claims.case_section: 5. Evaluating Competing Donor Hypotheses Against Primary Lexicons
claims.short_label: East Anglian nannicking / nonnaks + expressive ch-/sh- and Gold Rush -igan donor hypothesis
claims.statement: East Anglian dialect 'nannicking' ('full of tricks', 1815) and 'nannaken' / 'nonnaks' ('none 'a yar nonnaks', 1823–1866), augmented by expressive 'ch-'/'sh-' prefixation and mock-Irish '-igan' remodeling (cf. 1903 'shenannikin'), provides the closest attested phonological and semantic donor base, though bare American '*nannick' remains unattested.
claims.rationale: Essex/Suffolk/Norfolk glossaries (CERT-1700-301..304) match both stem phonology and idiomatic syntax, while Farmer & Henley's 'SHENANNIKIN' (CERT-1700-305) preserves /-kɪn/, but Dialect Notes (1893, CERT-1700-305) confirms zero pre-1854 American print tokens of unprefixed '*nannick'.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Pre-1854 British dialectal /ˈnænɪkɪn/ ('playing tricks') and idiomatic parallel 'none 'a yar nonnaks'.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Attested pre-1854 American print survival of bare '*nannick' prior to 'ch-'/'sh-' prefixation.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: Whether Yankee sailors or Gold Rush miners preserved oral 'nannicking' before prefixing 'ch-'/'sh-'.

limitations: Zero pre-1854 American print tokens of bare '*nannick' are currently known.
resolution_criteria: Locate pre-1854 American print/manuscript 'nannick(ing)' or transitional '*sh-nannikin'.

evidence.reason: 1 March 1815 Monthly Magazine Essex dialect 'Nannicking' ('full of tricks and antics').
1823 Moor Suffolk 'nannaken' and 'none 'a yar nonnaks'.
1830 Forby 'NONNOCK' and 1895 Rye '*Nonnecking'.
1866 Nall 'Nonnaken' and 1903 Wright EDD 'NANNICK'.
Records 1903 'SHENANNIKIN' and 1893 New England 'shenanigan' while noting zero bare American '*nannick' tokens.
Aligns with initial '<ch->' and trickery sense of 1854 'chenanigan'.

claims.case_section: 5. Evaluating Competing Donor Hypotheses Against Primary Lexicons
claims.short_label: Critique of Irish 'sionnachuighim', German 'schinageln', Spanish 'chanada', French 'manigance', and Algonquian lore
claims.statement: Primary foreign lexicons expose Webster's Second's 'sionnachuighim' as a 1904 Dinneen 1sg headword absent in Hiberno-English, show German Rotwelsch 'Schinagel-'/'Schenigelei' meant 'hard labor/work' rather than 'trick', find zero Mexican Spanish currency for Peninsular 'chanada', confirm no French '*chicanigance' bridge, and refute Algonquian 'fox' lore.
claims.rationale: Inspection of O'Brien/O'Reilly/Dinneen/Joyce (CERT-1700-306..309), Pfister/Avé-Lallemant/Kluge (310..312), Salvá/RAE/Ramos i Duarte (313, 314), Académie française (315), and Trumbull's Natick Dictionary (316) isolates specific lexical, semantic, or geographic defects in each competing proposal while leaving mock-Irish '-igan' cadence open as secondary reinforcement.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Refutation of literal 1sg 'sionnachuighim' borrowing and Algonquian 'fox' myths, and demonstration of semantic/geographic gaps in German, Spanish, and French donor proposals.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Exclusion of secondary mock-Irish '-igan' suffixal reinforcement or minor bilingual convergence.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: Whether oral Pacific port Spanish ever contributed secondary '<ch->' reinforcement to 1854 'chenanigan'.

limitations: Distinguishes refuted Algonquian/1sg-headword claims from weakened German, Spanish, and French scholarly hypotheses.

evidence.reason: Shows 1sg 'Sionnachuighim' is Dinneen's 1904 lemma convention and absent in Foley (1855).
Confirms zero Hiberno-English tokens in Joyce (1910).
Verifies 1768 O'Brien 'SEANNACHAIGHIM' ('play the fox').
Verifies 1817 O'Reilly 'Seannachaighim' / 'Sionnach'.
Shows 1812 Pfister / 1836 Schmeller 'Schienägel' meant convict/farm toil.
Shows 1862 Avé-Lallemant 'schinageln' meant post-1854 wheelbarrow labor.
Proves post-1873 Linke 'Schenigelei' meant 'Arbeit, Kunst' ('work, trade'), not 'trick'.
Verifies Peninsular Spanish 'CHANADA' ('trick', 1847/1852) lacking '-igan'.
Confirms zero entry for 'chanada' in Velázquez (1852) and Mexican Spanish Ramos i Duarte (1895).
Shows 1835 French 'CHICANE'/'MANIGANCE' lack any blended bridge to '-igan'.
Refutes Algonquian 'fox' conjecture via Trumbull's 1903 'wonkqussis'.
